definition:
Jesus gave his church two practices that it has kept in every century and every land: baptism, the washing with water in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit by which a person is marked as belonging to Christ, and the Lord's Supper, the meal of bread and cup by which his people remember his death, share in him and in one another, and look for his return. Paul hands on the words of the Supper as something he “received from the Lord” (1 Corinthians 11:23), and the risen Jesus sends his disciples to “make disciples of all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19). Both practices have deep roots in the Old Testament, in circumcision, the Passover, the crossing of the sea, and the covenant meals of Israel. Christians call them sacraments or ordinances. They agree that Christ commanded them; they differ, sometimes sharply, on who should be baptized and how, and on how Christ is present in the Supper. Those are second-order questions, matters that divide faithful churches without dividing the faith.

The word ‘sacrament’ comes from the Latin sacramentum, a pledge or a soldier's oath, which the Old Latin and Vulgate Bibles used to translate the Greek mystērion, ‘mystery’ or ‘revealed secret’ (as in Ephesians 5:32). Many Baptists and other free churches prefer ‘ordinance’, a practice ordained by Christ. The Greek verb baptizō means ‘to dip’ or ‘immerse’, and it could also mean ‘to wash’: Mark 7:4 and Luke 11:38 use it of ritual washing before meals, and the Greek Old Testament uses it of Naaman dipping himself in the Jordan (2 Kings 5:14). Its range matters to the debate over mode. The Supper is called “the Lord's Supper” (kyriakon deipnon, 1 Corinthians 11:20), “the breaking of bread” (Acts 2:42), and the Eucharist, from eucharisteō, ‘to give thanks’, since Jesus “gave thanks” over the bread (1 Corinthians 11:24). Paul calls the cup and bread a koinōnia, ‘participation’ or ‘sharing’, in Christ's blood and body (1 Corinthians 10:16), and Jesus asks that it be done in anamnēsis, ‘remembrance’ (Luke 22:19). In the Hebrew Bible the key words are ’ot, ‘sign’ (Genesis 9:12; 17:11), zikkaron, ‘memorial’ (Exodus 12:14), and berit, ‘covenant’.
ot:
From the beginning God attached visible signs to his promises. After the flood he set the rainbow in the clouds as “the sign of the covenant” (Genesis 9:12). When he made his covenant with Abraham he gave circumcision: “this will be a sign of the covenant between Me and you” (Genesis 17:11), to be given to every male in the household at eight days old (Genesis 17:12). Paul later calls it “a seal of the righteousness that he had by faith” (Romans 4:11), so that a sign could both mark membership in God's people and point to the faith that receives God's promise. The law itself taught that the outward sign was not enough. Moses commands, “Circumcise your hearts” (Deuteronomy 10:16), and promises that “The LORD your God will circumcise your hearts” (Deuteronomy 30:6); Jeremiah repeats the call (Jeremiah 4:4). Signs without the reality they signify were never what God wanted, and the prophets condemned worship performed while the heart was far from him (Isaiah 1:13).

The Passover is the most important background to the Lord's Supper. On the night of the exodus, each household killed a lamb, put its blood on the doorframe, and ate it in haste (Exodus 12). God said, “when I see the blood, I will pass over you” (Exodus 12:13), and commanded that the day be “a memorial for you” (Exodus 12:14), kept every year. The meal was built to teach: “When your children ask you, ‘What does this service mean to you?’” (Exodus 12:26), the parents were to tell the story of deliverance. In later Jewish practice the Passover meal included bread, wine, and words explaining each element, so that each generation was to see itself as brought out of Egypt. The Passover was also guarded: only the circumcised could eat it (Exodus 12:48), a link between the sign of entry and the covenant meal that shapes later Christian discussion of who may come to the Table. At Sinai, Moses sprinkled the people with blood and said, “This is the blood of the covenant that the LORD has made with you” (Exodus 24:8), and then the elders “saw the God of Israel” and “ate and drank” in his presence (Exodus 24:10-11). Jesus' words over the cup echo that scene directly.

Other threads anticipate baptism. Paul says Israel was “baptized into Moses in the cloud and in the sea” (1 Corinthians 10:2) when they passed through the waters out of slavery (Exodus 14:21-22), and Peter sees the ark that carried Noah's family through the flood as a picture of baptism (1 Peter 3:20-21). The priests washed before serving (Exodus 29:4), and the law's many washings for impurity taught that people must be made clean to approach God. The prophets promised a cleansing only God could give: “I will also sprinkle clean water on you, and you will be clean” (Ezekiel 36:25), joined in the next verses to a new heart and God's own Spirit, and Zechariah foresaw “a fountain” opened “to cleanse them from sin and impurity” (Zechariah 13:1). The manna, “bread from heaven” (Exodus 16:4), and the water from the rock fed Israel in the wilderness, and Paul calls them “spiritual food” and “spiritual drink” (1 Corinthians 10:3-4). Isaiah foresaw a feast for all peoples on God's mountain, where God “will swallow up death forever” (Isaiah 25:6-8). Melchizedek, the priest-king who “brought out bread and wine” to Abram (Genesis 14:18), was read by some early Christian writers, such as Cyprian of Carthage in his letter on the cup (Letter 63), as a figure of the Supper, though the New Testament itself does not make that connection. By the time of Jesus, Jews practiced ritual immersion in stepped pools (miqva'ot), many of which archaeologists have found in Jerusalem and at Qumran; whether Jews also baptized Gentile converts as early as the first century is debated among scholars.
nt:
John the Baptist appeared “preaching a baptism of repentance for the forgiveness of sins” (Mark 1:4), and people came “confessing their sins” (Mark 1:5). He said his baptism with water pointed to one who would “baptize you with the Holy Spirit and with fire” (Matthew 3:11). Jesus himself was baptized by John, not because he needed repentance but “to fulfill all righteousness” (Matthew 3:15), and as he came up from the water the Spirit descended and the Father spoke (Matthew 3:16-17), so that his baptism reveals the Father, the Son, and the Spirit together. Jesus' disciples baptized during his ministry (John 4:1-2). He spoke of his coming death as a baptism he must undergo (Mark 10:38), and after his resurrection he commanded baptism in the triune name as part of making disciples (Matthew 28:19). In Acts, baptism follows the preaching of the gospel at once. At Pentecost Peter says, “Repent and be baptized, every one of you, in the name of Jesus Christ for the forgiveness of your sins, and you will receive the gift of the Holy Spirit” (Acts 2:38), adding, “This promise belongs to you and your children and to all who are far off” (Acts 2:39). Samaritans, an Ethiopian official, Cornelius and his household, Lydia “and her household” (Acts 16:15), and the Philippian jailer “and all his household” (Acts 16:33) are baptized. Paul was told, “Get up, be baptized, and wash your sins away, calling on His name” (Acts 22:16). Acts 8:37, the eunuch's confession, is absent from the earliest manuscripts, which is why many English Bibles, including the BSB, omit it or place it in a note.

The letters explain what baptism means. It unites a person with Christ in his death and resurrection: “all of us who were baptized into Christ Jesus were baptized into His death” (Romans 6:3), “buried with Him through baptism into death” so that we may “walk in newness of life” (Romans 6:4). It clothes a person with Christ (Galatians 3:27) and joins him to the one body, for “in one Spirit we were all baptized into one body” (1 Corinthians 12:13). There is “one Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Ephesians 4:5). Paul links it with circumcision, a circumcision “performed by Christ and not by human hands” (Colossians 2:11), “having been buried with Him in baptism” and raised “through your faith” (Colossians 2:12). Titus 3:5 speaks of “the washing of new birth and renewal by the Holy Spirit”, and Peter says the water of the flood “symbolizes the baptism that now saves you also—not the removal of dirt from the body, but the pledge of a clear conscience toward God—through the resurrection of Jesus Christ” (1 Peter 3:21). Paul also warns the Corinthians against making baptism a badge of human loyalty: “Christ did not send me to baptize, but to preach the gospel” (1 Corinthians 1:17).

The Lord's Supper was instituted at a Passover meal on the night Jesus was betrayed. Matthew, Mark, and Luke record it, and Paul's account in 1 Corinthians 11, written around AD 53 to 55, is the earliest. Jesus “took bread, spoke a blessing and broke it, and gave it to the disciples, saying, ‘Take and eat; this is My body’” (Matthew 26:26). Over the cup he said, “This is My blood of the covenant, which is poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins” (Matthew 26:28), echoing Exodus 24:8, and in Luke and Paul, “This cup is the new covenant in My blood” (Luke 22:20), echoing Jeremiah's promise of a new covenant (Jeremiah 31:31-34). Jesus added, “do this in remembrance of Me” (Luke 22:19), and promised that he would drink the fruit of the vine anew in his Father's kingdom (Matthew 26:29). Part of Luke's account (Luke 22:19b-20) is missing from Codex Bezae and a few Old Latin manuscripts, but most textual scholars accept it as original. In John 6, after feeding the five thousand, Jesus calls himself “the bread of life” (John 6:35) and says, “unless you eat the flesh and drink the blood of the Son of Man, you have no life in you” (John 6:53), then adds, “The Spirit gives life; the flesh profits nothing” (John 6:63). Interpreters differ on whether the discourse speaks directly of the Supper or of faith, which the Supper later signs. At Emmaus the risen Jesus was “recognized” by two disciples “in the breaking of the bread” (Luke 24:35).

The first church devoted itself “to the breaking of bread and to prayer” (Acts 2:42), and at Troas believers gathered “On the first day of the week” “to break bread” (Acts 20:7). Paul teaches that “the bread that we break” is “a participation in the body of Christ” and that “Because there is one loaf, we who are many are one body” (1 Corinthians 10:16-17); for that reason believers cannot share both “the table of the Lord and the table of demons” (1 Corinthians 10:21). In Corinth the rich ate and drank while the poor went hungry, and Paul says bluntly, “it is not the Lord's Supper you eat” (1 Corinthians 11:20). He reminds them that “as often as you eat this bread and drink this cup, you proclaim the Lord's death until He comes” (1 Corinthians 11:26), warns that eating “in an unworthy manner” is sin “against the body and blood of the Lord” (1 Corinthians 11:27), and calls each to examine himself and to recognize the body (1 Corinthians 11:28-29). The Bible's story ends at a meal: “Blessed are those who are invited to the marriage supper of the Lamb” (Revelation 19:9).

keyTexts.why: Circumcision is given as the sign of God's covenant with Abraham and his household. The main Old Testament background for baptism and for the debate over whether children receive the sign.
The Passover lamb, the blood on the doorposts, and the memorial meal kept every year and explained to children. The meal within which Jesus instituted the Supper.
The blood of the covenant is sprinkled on the people, and the elders eat and drink in God's presence. Jesus' words over the cup echo this scene.
God promises to sprinkle clean water, give a new heart, and put his Spirit within his people. A prophetic picture of the cleansing baptism signifies.
Jesus is baptized by John, the Spirit descends, and the Father speaks. Baptism is joined to the revelation of the Trinity from the start.
The institution of the Supper: this is my body, this is my blood of the covenant, until I drink it new in my Father's kingdom.
The risen Christ commands baptism in the name of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit as part of making disciples of all nations.
Jesus the bread of life speaks of eating his flesh and drinking his blood. Read by some as eucharistic and by others as a picture of faith.
Repent and be baptized, the promise for you and your children, and a church devoted to the breaking of bread. Baptism and Supper in the first Christian community.
Lydia and her household, and the jailer and all his household, are baptized. Central to the debate over household baptism.
Baptism into Christ's death and resurrection. The fullest statement of what baptism signifies.
Israel was baptized into Moses in the sea and ate spiritual food. Paul reads the exodus as a pattern of the Christian signs and as a warning against trusting them without faith.
The cup and bread are a participation in Christ's blood and body, and the one loaf makes many one body.
The earliest account of the Supper, set against Corinth's divisions. It proclaims the Lord's death until he comes and calls for self-examination.
A circumcision not done by hands, buried with Christ in baptism and raised through faith. The key text linking the two signs.

history:
The earliest church order outside the New Testament, the Didache (usually dated between about AD 50 and 120), instructs that baptism be given in the triune name in running water, or by pouring water on the head three times if enough water is lacking (chapter 7), gives thanksgiving prayers for the cup and bread, and restricts the Eucharist to the baptized (chapters 9 and 10). Justin Martyr's First Apology (about 155, chapters 61 and 65 to 67) describes baptism, which he calls illumination, and the Sunday gathering at which the bread and cup are received not as common food. Tertullian's On Baptism (about 200) counseled delaying the baptism of small children, while the Apostolic Tradition traditionally attributed to Hippolytus (its date and authorship are debated, with many placing it in the early third century) directs that children be baptized first, with parents speaking for those who cannot answer. Origen and Cyprian of Carthage in the third century treat infant baptism as established practice. When Donatists in North Africa refused to recognize sacraments given by clergy who had lapsed under persecution, Augustine argued (in writings of about 400 to 411) that the sacrament belongs to Christ and is valid whatever the minister's worthiness, and he described a sacrament as a visible word, the word joined to the element (Tractates on John 80). In the ninth century two monks of Corbie, Paschasius Radbertus and Ratramnus, wrote treatises on the body and blood of the Lord that differed on how the bread is Christ's body, and Berengar of Tours was made to recant his symbolic view in 1059 and 1079. The Fourth Lateran Council (1215) used the word transubstantiation, Thomas Aquinas developed the doctrine (Summa Theologiae III, question 75), Peter Lombard's Sentences (about 1150s) had already fixed the number of sacraments at seven, and the Council of Florence (1439) confirmed that number.

The Reformation divided the Western church over the sacraments. Martin Luther's The Babylonian Captivity of the Church (1520) rejected the sacrifice of the Mass and reduced the sacraments to those Christ instituted with a visible sign and a promise, while holding firmly to the real presence of Christ's body and blood in, with, and under the bread and wine. Huldrych Zwingli in Zurich taught that the Supper is a memorial and pledge. The two met at the Marburg Colloquy in October 1529, agreed on fourteen of fifteen articles, and parted over the Supper. On 21 January 1525 Conrad Grebel baptized George Blaurock in Zurich, and the Anabaptist movement that followed, summarized in the Schleitheim Confession (1527), baptized only confessing believers. The Augsburg Confession (1530, Articles 9, 10, and 13) set out the Lutheran position. John Calvin (Institutes, Book 4, chapters 14 to 17, final edition 1559) taught that the sacraments are signs and seals of God's promises and that believers truly feed on Christ by the Spirit, and he and Heinrich Bullinger reached agreement for the Swiss Reformed churches in the Consensus Tigurinus (1549). The Council of Trent affirmed seven sacraments (session 7, 1547), transubstantiation (session 13, 1551), and the Mass as a true sacrifice (session 22, 1562). The Heidelberg Catechism (1563, questions 65 to 82), the Thirty-Nine Articles of the Church of England (Articles 25 to 28, 1563 and 1571), and the Westminster Confession (1646, chapters 27 to 29) set out Reformed and Anglican teaching, each retaining infant baptism and rejecting transubstantiation.

The English Baptists began when John Smyth baptized himself and his congregation in Amsterdam in 1609, and the Particular Baptists' First London Confession (1644) specified baptism by immersion; the Second London Confession (1689, chapters 28 to 30) calls baptism and the Supper ordinances and teaches that worthy receivers spiritually feed on Christ. John Wesley urged Methodists to frequent communion in his sermon The Duty of Constant Communion (published 1787). Two movements set outward sacraments aside altogether: the Society of Friends (Quakers) from the 1650s, and the Salvation Army from 1883, both holding that the inward reality is what matters, a practice other churches have not accepted. The Eastern Orthodox churches, which speak of the holy mysteries and commonly count seven, baptize infants by triple immersion and give them chrismation (anointing with oil) and communion at once. In the twentieth century the Second Vatican Council's Constitution on the Sacred Liturgy (1963) encouraged fuller participation of the people, and the World Council of Churches' Faith and Order document Baptism, Eucharist and Ministry (1982, the Lima text) recorded convergence and remaining disagreement among many traditions. The site's page on the sacraments presents the positions on baptism and the Supper at full strength.

differ.body: Christ gave his church seven sacraments (baptism, confirmation or chrismation, the Eucharist, penance, anointing of the sick, holy orders, and marriage), through which he truly gives the grace they signify. Baptism washes away sin and gives new birth by water and the Spirit (John 3:5; Titus 3:5), and so is given to infants of believing families, as household baptisms and the church's early practice show. In the Eucharist the bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ; Catholic teaching names this change transubstantiation, while the Orthodox affirm the change without defining how it happens. The Eucharist makes present the one sacrifice of Christ, not a new one. The sacraments act by the power of Christ, not by the worthiness of minister or recipient, though the recipient must not block grace by unbelief or grave sin. Defenders point to Jesus' words “this is My body,” to John 6, and to the realism of the early fathers.

Lutherans hold that God's Word joined to water, bread, and wine makes a sacrament, and that the sacraments are means by which God gives forgiveness, life, and salvation, received by faith. Baptism is a washing of rebirth (Titus 3:5) that truly saves (1 Peter 3:21), and so it is given to infants, whom God can bring to faith by his Word. In the Supper the true body and blood of Christ are present in, with, and under the bread and wine, and are received by all who eat, to blessing by those who believe and to judgment by those who do not (1 Corinthians 11:27-29). Lutherans reject transubstantiation as an unnecessary theory and reject any memorial view as denying Christ's plain words. The comfort of their view is that the gift does not depend on the strength of the receiver's faith; Christ gives himself “for you,” as the words of institution say.

The sacraments are signs and seals of the covenant of grace, visible promises by which God confirms his word to believers and through which the Holy Spirit truly nourishes faith. Baptism signifies union with Christ, cleansing, and new birth, and, because God's covenant promises have always included the children of believers (Genesis 17:7; Acts 2:39), it is given to them as circumcision was, without claiming that the water itself regenerates. In the Supper Christ's body is in heaven, but believers truly feed on the whole Christ by the Spirit through faith, a real communion rather than a bare memorial (1 Corinthians 10:16). Calvin and the Westminster Confession reject both transubstantiation and the Lutheran teaching that Christ's body is present everywhere the Supper is celebrated, holding that Christ's human body remains in heaven (Acts 3:21). Anglican and many Methodist teaching stands close to this view.

Baptism and the Lord's Supper are ordinances Christ commanded, powerful signs of the gospel for those who have received it. Baptism belongs to those who have repented and believed, since every baptism in the New Testament follows faith and the new covenant is made with those who know the Lord (Jeremiah 31:34). Most in this tradition baptize by immersion, the plain sense of baptizō and the picture of burial and resurrection in Romans 6:4. Baptism does not save by itself but is a believer's public confession and pledge, “the pledge of a clear conscience toward God” (1 Peter 3:21). The Supper is a covenant meal of remembrance and proclamation (1 Corinthians 11:24-26) in which the church renews its commitment and expresses its unity. Some in this tradition understand Christ as present by his Spirit among his gathered people, and the Second London Confession teaches a spiritual feeding on Christ; others stress the memorial. All reject the idea that grace is conveyed through the elements apart from faith.

errors:
The church has rejected distortions on both sides. One treats the sacraments as automatic, as if water or bread worked like a charm regardless of faith, repentance, or life. Paul warned the Corinthians that Israel had its own ‘baptism’ in the sea and its own spiritual food and drink, and yet “God was not pleased with most of them” (1 Corinthians 10:5), and he told them that their divided, selfish meal was not the Lord's Supper at all (1 Corinthians 11:20). Every major tradition, including those that hold the sacraments truly confer grace, teaches that unbelief receives them to its harm, not its good. The opposite distortion treats the signs as unimportant, optional customs that a spiritual Christian can take or leave. Christ commanded both, and the New Testament churches practiced both from the first day. The church has also rejected Donatism, the teaching that a sacrament's validity depends on the holiness of the minister, because the sacrament is Christ's act and not the minister's achievement, and it has rejected rebaptism of those already baptized in the triune name wherever it judged their baptism true, a judgment on which baptist and paedobaptist churches still differ.

Other errors are pastoral. The Supper can become a battleground for rivalry and exclusion within a single congregation, the very sin Paul rebuked in Corinth. Baptism can be sought for a child as a family custom with no intention of raising the child in the faith, or received by an adult as a moment of feeling rather than a pledge of lifelong discipleship. And the divisions between traditions, however sincerely held, can harden into contempt, when every tradition confesses that there is one Lord, one faith, and one baptism.
life:
Baptism tells a person who they are. Whatever a Christian feels on a given day, the water declares that he has been joined to Christ, buried with him and raised with him, and belongs to a people larger than any family, nation, or party (Galatians 3:27-28). Martin Luther's Large Catechism (1529) counsels the Christian troubled by sin and conscience to answer that he has been baptized and so holds God's promise, and Christians of every tradition have found in their baptism a fixed point outside their own changing feelings. Baptism also gives the church a common identity: rich and poor, Jew and Gentile, slave and free go into the same water.

The Supper shapes the rhythm of Christian life. It turns believers back to the cross (“you proclaim the Lord's death”), gathers them around one table where no one is more worthy than another, and points them forward to a feast still to come (“until He comes”, 1 Corinthians 11:26). It calls for self-examination but not for perfection; the Table is for sinners who need grace, not for those who have outgrown the need. For a person in grief, doubt, or failure, the bread and cup are something to receive when there is little left to offer, and for a divided church they are a standing rebuke and a standing hope.
questions: How do circumcision and the Passover help explain what baptism and the Lord's Supper mean, and where does the New Testament show that the new signs go beyond the old ones?

Paul says the Corinthians' meal was not really the Lord's Supper because of how they treated the poor (1 Corinthians 11:17-22). What does that suggest about the connection between the Table and the way a church lives together?

The traditions described here disagree on who should be baptized and how Christ is present at the Table. What do they all affirm, and how should that shape the way Christians who disagree treat one another?
